status_summary: EO 14317 (signed 2025-07-17) created Schedule G for noncareer policy-making or policy-advocating positions with no numerical cap, OPM guidance of 2025-07-29 gives the White House Presidential Personnel Office final review of placements, and OPM proposed on 2026-09-18 to codify Schedule G in the excepted-service regulations. The Partnership for Public Service reported (report dated 2026-03-23, data through 2026-01-31) 1,835 Schedule C and 770 noncareer SES appointees, the highest Schedule C count in its historical table and 8 below the noncareer SES record, with political appointees filling 11.7 percent of filled SES positions and career SES falling from 8,127 to 5,837; Schedule G appointees were not counted. Senate-confirmed posts are the lagging part: a July 2026 Partnership analysis reported the fewest nominations of any president since Reagan and 27 confirmed officials already departed. On the SES side, a presidential memorandum of 2025-01-20 directed agencies to reconstitute Performance Review Boards and to have senior noncareer officials chair and form a majority of Executive Resources Boards, and OPM memos of 2025-02-04 (chief information officer posts) and 2025-02-24 (all career-reserved posts) asked agencies to request redesignation of career-reserved SES positions as general, with requests due 2025-03-24; a May 2026 CRS report describes these steps as ones that would lead to some redesignations but gives no count, and no list of approved redesignations was found. A government-wide civilian hiring freeze ordered on 2025-01-20 was followed by EO 14356 (2025-10-15), which requires agency strategic hiring committees to approve career vacancies, broader than the Mandate's freeze on top career hiring, and exempts noncareer SES, Schedule C and Schedule G positions. The White House Cabinet page (modified 2026-10-01) does not list the OPM Director.

timeline.event: A presidential memorandum froze hiring of federal civilian employees government-wide, with exceptions including national security and public safety; Senate-confirmed presidential appointments, noncareer SES and Schedule C appointments were excluded from the freeze (extension tracked in c06-10).

A presidential memorandum on career senior executives (90 FR 8481, published 2025-01-30) directs agencies to end existing Executive Resources Boards and form new ones chaired by, and with a majority of, senior noncareer officials alongside career members, and to reconstitute Performance Review Boards with members committed to enforcing SES evaluations.
OPM asks agencies to request redesignation of career-reserved chief information officer SES positions as general so that noncareer appointees may fill them (as described by CRS).

OPM's Acting Director asks agencies to review career-reserved SES positions and, by 2025-03-24, submit a revised list and requests to redesignate the rest as general, starting with posts at deputy assistant secretary level and above; the memo notes a statutory floor of 3,571 career-reserved positions and says the count has grown to about double that.

EO 14317 creates Schedule G in the excepted service for noncareer positions of a policy-making or policy-advocating character that normally change with a presidential transition; no numerical cap in the order, and Civil Service Rules on removal do not apply except as statute requires.
OPM issues Schedule G guidance: agencies coordinate through OPM's Executive and Schedule C System, and final review and approval rests with the White House Office of Presidential Personnel.

OPM SES rule published (effective 2025-10-15); OPM may exclude noncareer SES members from forced distribution, and Performance Review Board language shifts from diversity to commitment to the appraisal system. It does not address career-reserved positions or PRB composition.

EO 14356 requires strategic hiring committees (deputy agency head, chief of staff and designees) to approve each vacancy filled or created, plus annual staffing plans; noncareer SES, Schedule C and Schedule G positions are excluded from its limits.

The Partnership for Public Service reports, with data through 2026-01-31, 1,835 Schedule C and 770 noncareer SES appointees (a Schedule C high and 8 below the noncareer SES record), political appointees at 11.7 percent of filled SES positions, and career SES down from 8,127 to 5,837; Schedule G is not counted.

CRS report R48932 describes the 2025 OPM memos as steps that would result in some career-reserved positions becoming general but gives no count of completed redesignations; it reports 6,647 SES members as of April 2026, down from about 8,780 in September 2024.

Government Executive reports a Partnership for Public Service analysis: 27 Senate-confirmed officials (11.4 percent) have left, more than at the same point in the first term, nominations are the fewest since Reagan, and acting officials have increased.

OPM proposes a rule that adds Schedule G to excepted-service regulations and treats it like Schedule C for several purposes (exclusion from performance-based removal procedures, counting as political appointments, SES conversion rules).
The White House Cabinet page, whose metadata shows a modification date of 2026-10-01 and which was read on 2026-10-07, lists 21 Cabinet members and does not list the OPM Director.

title: Staff political appointee ranks and limit career control of policy positions
uncertainties: Appointee counts come from one nonprofit report (data through 2026-01-31) and a secondary article; a second article dated 2026-04-27 gives the Schedule C count as of the end of 2025, so the exact count date differs by source. No official OPM count of Schedule G placements was found. The statement that political appointees exceed any past share of SES is the Partnership report's characterization. The Cabinet-page finding reflects one page read on 2026-10-07 and does not show whether the OPM Director attends Cabinet meetings. OPM memos of 2025-02-04 and 2025-02-24 sought redesignation of career-reserved SES positions as general, and CRS (R48932, 2026-05-01) says these steps would result in some redesignations, but no count of approved redesignations was found; the latest Federal Register list of career-reserved positions found covers calendar year 2024 (published 2025-05-20). Whether reconstituted Executive Resources Boards are in fact chaired by noncareer officials at each agency was not checked. Not re-checked: the 2025 Senate rule change on en bloc confirmations (tracked in c01-03). The stage is implemented because the core mechanisms (Schedule G, record noncareer appointments, White House approval of placements, noncareer-led Executive Resources Boards) are operative, while the Senate-confirmed cadre, Cabinet status and completed career-reserved redesignations are not shown.
